q7.answer: The clients no longer copy a key at construction. For every outbound call they ask the in-memory secret holder (secrets.get('<name>')), which returns the key from the current snapshot. The refresh thread swaps in a new snapshot atomically, so the next call uses the new key. A call already in flight finishes with the key it started with.

q8.answer: Each replica reports the version id it holds for each of the three secrets, on an internal-only endpoint or metric (ids only, never values). The on-call or release engineer checks that no pod runs a pre-migration image and that every replica's ids match the ids recorded when the keys were written in step 3. Any mismatch blocks revocation. The team waits for the 5-minute refresh, re-checks, and restarts the pod if it still differs. A soak window and an inventory of other users of the old keys follow before revocation.

q9.answer: Order: (1) set store access and policies and test them; (2) issue new keys at the providers while the old keys stay active; (3) write the new keys to the prod store; (4) pre-flight check the new keys. The PR is written in parallel but not deployed until step 4 passes. The single PR does the app switch, the removal of api_key from config/app.yaml and the CI guard together. After staging drills pass it is merged and rolled out. Then come confirmation that every instance is on the new keys, a soak window, and revocation of the old keys. Rotation therefore happens before the switch, and revocation is last. Removing keys from the file is part of the same PR as the switch to the store, not a separate step.

q10.answer: Local runs (make run) set APP_ENV=dev and fetch keys from the dev store paths (orders-api/dev/<name>), which hold provider sandbox or test keys. They use the engineer's own credentials, and the dev paths are readable by engineers. A make run-offline option uses local stub providers with no keys and no store call. Prod access is denied by policy, so a developer who tries APP_ENV=prod is refused and the app exits.

q11.answer: It treats a missing secret as a failed load. The app must have all three keys before it reports ready, so it counts it as a failed attempt and retries (4 attempts in all, 2 seconds apart). After the last attempt it logs the error class and the secret names (never values) and exits non-zero. /healthz stays 503, so in prod the rollout halts and the old pods keep serving.
